name: Iron supplements (oral)
short: A 2005 US study called iron a major cause of accidental poisoning death in young children; deaths fell after unit-dose packaging. Ferrous sulfate about doubled the odds of gut side effects vs placebo.
text: In a meta-analysis of 43 randomised trials with 6831 adults, ferrous sulfate taken by mouth significantly increased the risk of gastrointestinal side effects compared with placebo (odds ratio 2.32) and compared with intravenous iron (odds ratio 3.05), with no evidence of a relationship with dose; these findings concern ferrous sulfate, not every form of iron. Accidental overdose can be fatal in young children: a US study published in 2005 describes iron poisoning as a major cause of unintentional poisoning death in young children and reported that deaths among children under 6 recorded by poison control centres fell from 29 in the 10 years before unit-dose packaging of iron supplements was required to 1 in the 5 years after. Iron overload from supplements is documented in the cited sources only by a case report of a mother and daughter who took an over-the-counter amino acid chelated iron supplement (the abstract does not say for how long) and had raised ferritin and transferrin saturation, with iron accumulation in the liver, spleen and bone marrow on the daughter's MRI; after they stopped the over-the-counter products and had about two years of phlebotomy, their blood results showed a trend toward improvement, and the authors warn that iron overload can be present without symptoms. A systematic review of levothyroxine interactions found limited evidence that iron supplements, like calcium supplements and coffee, decrease levothyroxine absorption, and described keeping a time interval between them as an effective way to avoid this.
